newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania holds ceremony for parting security force.
newsitem.headline: Albania holds ceremony for parting security force.

text.p: Albania held a farewell ceremony on Friday for a multinational security force which has overseen aid deliveries since April and ensured free elections in the Balkan nation after months of unrest.
The Italian-led force of some 7,000 soldiers from 10 nations will pull out of Albania completely by August 11, leaving Europe's poorest nation relatively stable and on the road to recovery.

Albanian Defence Minister Sabit Brokaj and his Italian counterpart Beniamino Andreatta, who flew in for the occasion, inspected the troops before the multinational protection force flag was lowered at their base in Rinas, 25 km (15 miles) south of the capital Tirana.
"Our people are grateful to those countries which sent their sons to assist the Albanian people in these difficult times," Brokaj said.

Brokaj presented Albania's prestigious Mother Teresa Award to troop commander General Luciano Forlani, commending the mission's efforts, especially in assisting in the general election held on June 29.
In an emotional speech Andreatta said: "We are pleased our attempt to assist the Albanian people was successful. Albanians can again tread a path of democracy, peace and development."
The blazing sunshine under which the ceremony was held was a far cry from the cold, windy conditions that welcomed the troops' arrival in April.

Multinational troops were deployed across Albania in April in Operation Alba (Italian for dawn) after a violent uprising sparked by the collapse of get-rich-quick savings schemes left the army and police in disarray and state authority in tatters.
President Sali Berisha's Democratic government was forced to resign after he was blamed for allowing the shady investment funds, in which thousands lost their life savings, to flourish.
"We could not remain indifferent to the crises of a neighbouring ally," Andreatta said. "We could not ignore sufferings of a people, many of whom speak Italian."
The Socialist-led five-party coalition government has pledged to rebuild the country by reforming the police, the army and the financial system.
Andreatta said Italy was committed to assisting Albania.
"The Italian government is committed to helping to restructure Albania's armed forces and police because democracy must be protected," he said.

Lieutenant Colonel Giovanni Bernardi told Reuters that General Forlani would lead the last troops of the force out of Albania on Monday but a separate contingent would be sent to help in the reconstruction efforts.

The multinational force was criticised by some for not intervening to stop the violence of the past months, which has taken the death toll to over 1,500. Its U.N. mandate was only to protect humanitarian convoys.
Just one soldier died from a grenade explosion and up to eight others were slightly injured from stray bullets, Bernardi said.
